newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Sanctions against Libya continue after U.N. review.
newsitem.headline: Sanctions against Libya continue after U.N. review.

text.p: The Security Council, after a periodic review on Friday, left unchanged sanctions imposed on Libya in connection with a 1988 airliner bombing over Lockerbie, Scotland, that killed 270 people, council members said.

They said council President Nugroho Wisnumurti of Indonesia, after hearing members' views during closed-door consultations, repeated that there was no consensus for making any changes in the sanctions.

The punitive measures, which include an air embargo, a ban on arms sales and the downgrading of diplomatic relations, were first imposed in 1992 because of Libya's refusal to extradite two men accused of planting a bomb aboard Pan Am Flight 103, which exploded over the Scottish town.

The sanctions, reviewed by the council every 120 days, also penalise Libya for not cooperating in the investigation into the 1989 bombing of France's UTA Flight 772 over Niger, which killed all 171 aboard.

Because of Tripoli's continued non-compliance, the council imposed additional measures in 1993, including a freeze on some of Libya's assets abroad and a ban on its import of certain types of equipment used in oil transport terminals and refineries. But they do not affect the export of Libyan oil or its purchase of oil drilling equipment.

The two Lockerbie suspects, Abdel Baset Ali Mohamed al-Meghrahi and Al-Amin Khalifa Fhimah, have been indicted in Britain and the United States. Those countries demand they stand trial in a Scottish or U.S. court.

London and Washington have repeatedly rejected offers by Libya, backed by the Arab League, the Organisation of African Unity and the non-aligned movement, for them to be tried by a Scottish judge under Scottish law but at the World Court at The Hague. Libya says they could not get a fair trial in Britain or the United States.

U.S. ambassador Madeleine Albright, in a statement during the latest council review, said there was "absolutely no precedent for holding a trial on Scottish or U.S. criminal charges outside the country that brought the charges."
She called Libya's offer for the suspects to be tried elsewhere "an empty ruse that falls far short of full compliance with relevant Security Council resolutions."

"The will of the world community on this issue has never been clearer. We would betray that will, the will of the council, and most important, the families of the victims of Libyan-sponsored terrorism were we to retreat now into unwarranted and shameful compromise with a terrorist supporting state," said Albright, whose remarks were later made public.

In a letter to Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali in September, Libya said the sanctions had caused it economic losses totalling more than $18.7 billion between mid-April 1992 and the end of 1995.
It also said the inability to import medicines by air and to fly patients abroad for treatment had caused death and suffering to thousands of people.
